metadata.title: ROC Curve and AUC Score, Oversimplified
metadata.greeting_note: Ahoj (Czech) rotates away from Jambo, Ciao, Namaste, Bonjour, and Shalom in the current batch. Liam is in for Sanjiv; the channel handle is @Sanjiv.
metadata.color_semantics: Claude fidelity skin on B00/B07/B08/B09. B01-B06 are native Manim illustrations on cream with ink and one terracotta event accent. Warn is reserved for false alarms and the deployment-mismatch beat.
metadata.note: Fresh concept explainer. The one idea: ROC is the map of threshold tradeoffs; AUC compresses the map into ranking quality, not deployment quality. The worked example uses six explicitly schematic cases and computes 8 correctly ordered positive-negative pairs out of 9. UI appears only on the four bookends.

beats.narration_text: A classifier does not begin with yes or no. It begins with a score, and somebody has to decide where yes starts. This is Liam, in for Sanjiv. The ROC curve shows every tradeoff that decision can make. AUC compresses the whole curve into one ranking score. Useful, yes. A deployment decision, absolutely not. Let us separate the map from the number.

show.event: Claude composer opens on 'Ahoj, Liam'
the ROC/AUC question types into the composer
send arms; running text reads 'sweeping the threshold…'
answered lines land: curve = tradeoffs; area = ranking; threshold = your decision

props.command: Explain the significance of the ROC curve and AUC score. Show what changes as the classification threshold moves, what AUC measures, and what neither metric decides for me.
output: AUC → ranking quality in one number

beats.narration_text: Here is the whole idea in one breath. Move a classifier's threshold and you trade caught positives against false alarms. The ROC curve records that trade at every threshold. A curve pushed toward the upper-left separates the classes better. AUC summarizes that separation as the chance that a random positive outranks a random negative. It compares rankings across thresholds; it does not choose the threshold you should deploy.

show.event: spark line: 'Map first. Number second.'
a threshold slider sweeps left across two score rows
caught-positive and false-alarm counters rise together
their moving pair traces a ROC curve toward the upper-left
the area fills once, then the threshold marker remains separate

production_viz.label: threshold sweep to curve to area
production_viz.mechanic: one control creates a family of operating points; AUC summarizes their ranking

beats.narration_text: The framework has one moving part: the threshold. At each setting, count the positives you caught and divide by all actual positives. That is true positive rate. Count the negatives you falsely flagged and divide by all actual negatives. That is false positive rate. Plot false positive rate across, true positive rate up, and every threshold becomes one point. Sweep the threshold, and the points become the ROC curve.

show.event: spark line: 'One threshold. One point.'
threshold cuts a vertical ranked stack
TPTPR/positives builds beside FFP/negatives
the two rates become the coordinates (FPR, TPR)
four threshold positions place four connected points on the ROC axes

production_viz.label: one point per threshold
production_viz.mechanic: thresholded counts become FPR and TPR coordinates

beats.narration_text: Now use the framework on six cases, three positive and three negative, ranked by score. Start above everything: nobody is flagged, so the point is zero, zero. Lower the threshold. Each positive moves the curve up; each negative moves it right. In this ranking, only one negative jumps ahead of one positive. The staircase finishes at one, one, and eight of the nine positive-negative pairs are in the right order.

show.event: the B02 axes remain while six scored cases appear in ranked order: P P N P N N
threshold starts above the list at ROC point (0,0)
first two positives step the curve upward twice
the early negative steps right; the last positive steps up
remaining negatives step right to (1,1)
a 3×3 pair grid counts 8 correct, 1 inversion

production_viz.label: six-case ROC walk
production_viz.mechanic: P creates an up-step; N creates a right-step; pair grid verifies AUC = 8/9

beats.narration_text: Now the area earns its meaning. AUC is not the percent of predictions that are correct. It is the probability that a randomly chosen positive receives a higher score than a randomly chosen negative, with ties handled appropriately. Our example gets eight out of nine pair orderings right, so its AUC is about zero point eight nine. A random ranking averages zero point five. Perfect separation scores one.

show.event: spark line: 'AUC judges the ranking.'
the words 'percent correct' appear and are struck through
one positive-negative pair is drawn; the higher score wins
the 3×3 pair grid fills eight terracotta checks and one ink inversion
8 ÷ 9 resolves to 0.89 beside the shaded ROC area
0.5 random and 1.0 perfect anchors appear on a scale

production_viz.label: pairwise interpretation of AUC
production_viz.mechanic: correct positive-negative orderings equal the empirical ROC area

beats.narration_text: So which point on the curve should you use? The curve cannot answer until you price the mistakes. In a disease screen, missing a case may be costly, so you might accept more false alarms. In an expensive manual-review queue, false alarms consume people and time, so the useful region may be the far-left slice. Compare models there, then choose a threshold using real costs, capacity, and prevalence.

show.event: spark line: 'The curve needs a policy.'
one ROC curve appears with three candidate threshold dots
disease-screen branch enlarges the high-recall region
manual-review branch crops to the low-FPR region
cost + capacity + prevalence arrows converge on one chosen operating point

production_viz.label: same curve, two policies
production_viz.mechanic: different error costs select different regions and thresholds

beats.act: FALSIFIABILITY — a good AUC can still fail
beats.narration_text: Here is where one beautiful number lies by omission. AUC measures ordering across all thresholds. Your product uses one threshold, under one class balance, with one error budget. A model can rank well yet produce badly calibrated probabilities, overwhelm the queue with false positives, or fail a subgroup. And under severe imbalance, inspect precision-recall behavior too. High AUC is evidence of separation. It is not evidence that deployment is safe.

show.event: spark line: 'Ranking is not deployment.'
an AUC badge stays fixed at 0.89
three panels split beneath it: calibration, queue capacity, subgroup
each panel reveals a distinct failure despite the unchanged badge
an imbalanced positive/negative strip appears beside a precision-recall curve
the AUC badge relabels itself 'separation evidence — not safety'

production_viz.label: unchanged AUC, three deployment failures
production_viz.mechanic: ranking summary is held constant while calibration, capacity, and subgroup checks fail
production_viz.note: PR is an additional view under imbalance, not universally superior

beats.narration_text: Let us recap with Claude. A score becomes decisions only after you choose a threshold. Sweep that threshold and each true-positive-rate, false-positive-rate pair traces the ROC curve. A curve nearer the upper-left means stronger separation. AUC compresses the ranking into the chance that a random positive outranks a random negative. Use it to compare ranking quality. Then return to the curve, your operating region, calibration, and real-world costs before you deploy.

show.event: Claude verdict artifact opens with a compact ROC curve
threshold → point → curve sequence highlights
AUC definition lands beside a shaded area
deployment checklist reveals: region, calibration, costs
verdict line lands: 'A ranking score is not a policy.'

artifactLines: ROC — each threshold becomes one (false-positive rate, true-positive rate) point.
AUC — the chance a random positive outranks a random negative.
Use — compare ranking quality, then inspect the operating region you can afford.
The catch — ranking is not calibration, capacity, fairness, or deployment safety.

beats.narration_text: Your turn. Paste this in: take my classifier scores and labels, draw the ROC curve, calculate AUC, and mark the thresholds that keep false positive rate below my real capacity limit. For each marked point, report recall, precision, calibration, and the number of cases sent to review. Then check the answer. Did it use scores rather than hard labels? Did it name the positive class? And did it keep threshold choice separate from AUC?
